# OpenCodeRAG **A local-first toolkit that gives AI coding agents search, memory, judgment, and guardrails.** [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/opencode-rag-plugin.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-rag-plugin) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) AI coding agents are capable, but they have four recurring weaknesses: they read whole files to find one function, they forget everything between sessions, they interrupt you with questions they could settle themselves, and they may run risky shell commands without a second opinion. OpenCodeRAG addresses all these problems and more in one package: - **Semantic Search**: retrieval tools that find relevant code parts by a rough description only - **Persistent Memory**: vectorized memory, which keeps gotchas and decisions across sessions and automatically injects them into the context when necessary - **Knowledge Base**: agents use and maintain a project wiki to understand the code base better - **Basic Judgment**: a small local decision model that answers classification and routing questions - **Guardrails**: shell guard, which evaluates shell commands for malignancy before they run - **Image Description**: describes images with a local vision model for non-multimodal LLMs - **Documentation Assistant**: maintains and adds code documentation where it is still missing or unclear OpenCodeRAG is primarily built as an [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) plugin. But it can also be run as a MCP server for other AI coding platforms or used as a standalone command-line tool. By default it works fully locally via Ollama, but it can also use OpenAI-compatible APIs. No GPU is required, although it is recommended when using code and image descriptions. Smaller embedding models can still run fine on a modern CPU. --- ## Contents - [What you get](#what-you-get) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [How it works](#how-it-works) - [Ways to use it](#ways-to-use-it) - [Capabilities in detail](#capabilities-in-detail) - [1. Semantic code search](#1-semantic-code-search) - [2. Quirk memory](#2-quirk-memory) - [3. Decision model](#3-decision-model) - [4. Shell Guard](#4-shell-guard) - [5. Documentation and wiki modes](#5-documentation-and-wiki-modes) - [6. Image indexing](#6-image-indexing) - [7. Web UI, evaluation, and calibration](#7-web-ui-evaluation-and-calibration) - [Tool reference](#tool-reference) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Privacy and security](#privacy-and-security) - [Limitations](#limitations) - [Documentation index](#documentation-index) - [Contributing and support](#contributing-and-support) - [License](#license) --- ## What you get | Capability | What it does for your agent | On by default | |---|---|:---:| | **Search** | Finds the relevant code by meaning and by exact symbol name, instead of reading whole files | Yes | | **Memory** | Remembers gotchas, decisions, and past tool failures across sessions | Yes | | **Decisions** | Classifies, routes, and scores short text locally, without spending agent tokens | No | | **Protection** | Checks every shell command for destructive or malicious intent before it runs | No | | **Documentation** | Drives the agent to document undocumented code (`/doc`) and to maintain a project wiki (`/wiki`) | Wiki: yes, Doc: no | | **Vision** | Makes screenshots and diagrams searchable through generated descriptions | Yes | | **Measurement** | Tracks token use, retrieval quality, and decision accuracy, with a web dashboard | Tools, always available | **Why it is built this way** - **Fewer tokens.** The agent gets the handful of relevant chunks, not entire files. - **Search the way code is written.** AST-aware chunking keeps functions and classes intact. Hybrid vector and keyword search catches both meaning ("where is auth handled?") and exact names. - **Local by default.** Embeddings, the vector store, and the optional decision model run on your machine. No source code leaves the workspace unless you configure a hosted provider. - **Scales with the repository.** Incremental indexing and a background watcher keep the index current. An optional shared ClickHouse store supports large or multi-machine workspaces. --- ## Quick start > **Package name:** only install `opencode-rag-plugin`. The npm package `opencode-rag` is an unrelated, discontinued project by a different author. **Prerequisites:** Node.js v22+ and [Ollama](https://ollama.ai) (the default provider). OpenCode is optional; the CLI and MCP server work without it. ```bash # 1. Install the plugin and the CLI npm install -g opencode-rag-plugin # 2. Set up the runtime, the workspace, and your models # (a short interactive wizard guides you through the configuration; # the web UI then opens on the Configuration page) cd /path/to/your/project opencode-rag setup # 3. Build the index (may take a while) opencode-rag index # 4. Search from the terminal opencode-rag query "authentication middleware" ``` Example output: ``` Querying: "authentication middleware" Top-K: 10 Searching 1240 indexed chunks... 3 result(s) in 41ms: src/auth/middleware.ts:12-48 Score: 0.8123 ... ``` Open OpenCode in the same directory and the agent can use the tools right away.
What does opencode-rag setup do? It handles the whole onboarding in one command: - installs or verifies the machine-level runtime in `~/.opencode/` - scaffolds the current workspace (`.opencode/` config, plugin entries, skill files) - on the first run, or with `--reconfigure`, starts a **model wizard** for the embedding, description, vision, and decision models - an interactive run finishes by opening the **Web UI on its Configuration page**, so the generated settings can be reviewed and adjusted; the server stays up until you press `Ctrl+C` (`--no-ui` keeps setup headless) A plain re-run only syncs the workspace files. The wizard is scriptable (`--yes`, `--provider`, `--base-url`, `--embedding-model`, `--description off`, and more), and `--skip-runtime` limits the run to the workspace. Use `opencode-rag update` to upgrade the runtime to a newer release. `pnpm add -g`, `yarn global add`, and `bun add -g` work as drop-in replacements for npm. Setup and update detect which package manager owns the install.
### Optional add-ons These are off by default and can be enabled later: | Add-on | Enable with | Requires | |---|---|---| | [Shell Guard](#4-shell-guard) | `shellGuard.enabled` or `setup --shell-guard on` | tev1 via Ollama ≥ 0.35 | | [Decision model](#3-decision-model) | `decision.enabled` or `setup --decision on` | tev1 via Ollama ≥ 0.35 | | [Documentation mode](#documentation-mode-doc) | `documentationMode.enabled` | nothing extra | | [Shared ClickHouse Vector Database](doc/clickhouse.md) | `vectorStore.provider: "clickhouse"` or `setup --vector-store clickhouse` | a ClickHouse server | Two features are **on** by default and worth disabling if they do not fit your setup: [image descriptions](#6-image-indexing) (`imageDescription.enabled`, needs a vision model) and [wiki mode](#wiki-mode-wiki) (`wikiMode.enabled`). > **Contributors:** clone the repo and run `npm install --legacy-peer-deps; npm run build`. See the [development docs](doc/development.md). --- ## How it works ``` Workspace files │ tree-sitter chunking (AST-aware) ▼ Chunks ─────► embeddings ─────► vector store (LanceDB by default) │ └─────────► keyword index (TF×IDF) Query ─► vector search + keyword search ─► weighted fusion ─► top-K chunks ``` 1. **Index.** Files are split into semantic chunks, optionally described by a local LLM, embedded, and stored next to a TF×IDF keyword index. A file-hash manifest means only changed files are reprocessed, and a background watcher keeps the index current while you work. 2. **Retrieve.** The query is embedded and matched against both signals. The scores are fused and post-processed (deduplication, per-file chunk limits, adjacent-chunk merging) to fit the context window. 3. **Use.** The agent calls `search_semantic`, `get_file_skeleton`, or `find_usages` instead of reading entire files. The other capabilities build on the same foundation. For example, quirk memories are embedded and stored in the same vector store as your code. --- ## Ways to use it | Mode | Best for | How to start | |---|---|---| | **OpenCode plugin** | Day-to-day agent work with the full feature set (hotkeys, memory, Shell Guard, `/doc`, `/wiki`) | `opencode-rag setup`, then open OpenCode | | **MCP server** | Claude Desktop, Cursor, and any other MCP-compatible client | `opencode-rag mcp` | | **CLI** | Scripts, CI, and manual exploration | `opencode-rag ` | ### With OpenCode - **Discovery.** Workspace setup creates `.opencode/skills/opencode-rag/SKILL.md` (tool workflow) and `.opencode/skills/make-decision/SKILL.md` (decision-model guidance). Agents load them on demand, so idle sessions pay almost no token cost. When the index contains chunks, a brief tool list is also added to the system prompt. It is skipped when nothing is indexed. - **Hotkeys.** `Ctrl+Enter` appends a relevant file list to the prompt you are typing. `Ctrl+Alt+Enter` appends full code chunks. The query is taken from your typed text; if the prompt is empty, a toast reminds you to type first. Results land directly in the prompt as code blocks with file paths, line ranges, and relevance scores. - **Read override.** A normal `read` can return the file plus supplementary RAG chunks relevant to the surrounding work. - **Settings.** Models, retrieval options, and keybindings are configurable in the TUI settings panel (`Alt+S` or `/rag-settings`). - **`AGENTS.md` directive.** Workspace setup merges a tool-usage directive into `AGENTS.md` using sentinel markers. ### With other MCP clients ```bash opencode-rag mcp ``` The MCP server is only needed when an *external* client connects. Inside OpenCode the tools are registered in-process. The plugin auto-starts the server only when `mcp.enabled` is `true` (default `false`). Clients can also configure it manually, and workspace setup can register it for you. ### From the CLI ```bash opencode-rag setup # install the runtime, scaffold the workspace, run the model wizard opencode-rag index # build or update the index opencode-rag query "..." # search from the terminal opencode-rag status # index health and coverage opencode-rag ui # open the web dashboard ``` Further commands: `list`, `show `, `dump`, `clear`, `describe-image`, `decide`, `mcp`, `update`, `clickhouse`, `quirk`, and the `eval:*` family. Run `opencode-rag --help` or see the [CLI reference](doc/cli.md). --- ## Capabilities in detail ### 1. Semantic code search The core of the project. It answers natural-language queries with the most relevant code. - **Languages and formats.** AST chunking for 26 languages via tree-sitter, plus documents (Markdown, LaTeX, PDF, DOCX, Excel) and images. - **Hybrid search.** Vector similarity combined with TF×IDF keyword matching. The keyword index is repaired from the store whenever it drifts behind, so the keyword half never covers only part of the corpus. - **Context optimization.** Deduplication, per-file chunk limits, and adjacent-chunk merging. - **Configurable parsers.** Remap file extensions to any parser via `chunking.parsers` (for example `.c` → `cpp`). The override applies to chunking, `get_file_skeleton`, and read labels ([docs](doc/chunking.md#parser-overrides-per-extension-chunkingparsers)). - **Alternate providers.** Embeddings via Ollama, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, or Cohere. Descriptions and vision via Anthropic, Google Gemini, or OpenAI-compatible endpoints. - **Scale.** Incremental indexing, a background watcher, and automatic rebuild on corruption. The optional ClickHouse backend provides one shared index across machines and workspaces, with HNSW ANN, epoch rebuilds, and state sync ([docs](doc/clickhouse.md)). ### 2. Quirk memory Quirk memory gives the agent a **persistent, cross-session memory** of non-obvious facts: gotchas, preferences, decisions, and environment constraints. Quirks are embedded in the same vector store as your code and injected into the agent's context when their relevance clears a configurable threshold. The agent stops repeating the same mistake and accumulates project knowledge over time. **Enabled by default.** Configure it in `opencode-rag.json`: ```json { "memory": { "enabled": true, "autoInject": true, "minConfidence": 0.5, "recallMinScore": 0.72, "autoInjectMinScore": 0.75, "autoInjectTopK": 1, "autoInjectLatencyBudgetMs": 2000, "injectOnToolError": true, "autoCreateOnToolError": true, "toolErrorCreateMaxPerSession": 2, "decay": { "enabled": false, "halfLifeDays": 30 } } } ``` **Three ways memory works** | Mechanism | What happens | |---|---| | **Auto-injection** | On every user message, quirks related to the query and the agent's last response are injected if their vector similarity reaches `autoInjectMinScore` (0.75). Each quirk is injected at most once per session. A latency budget (`autoInjectLatencyBudgetMs`, 2000 ms) keeps a slow embedder from blocking messages. | | **Learning from failures** | When a tool call fails, the plugin looks for a matching quirk and injects it into the next request (`injectOnToolError`). If none exists, it writes one from a deterministic template built from the tool name and error text, with no LLM involved (`autoCreateOnToolError`). These quirks are tagged `tool-error`, kept for *future* sessions, and excluded from generic auto-injection. Creation is limited to 2 per session, with a 10-minute cooldown per error, and is skipped if a quirk for the same tool and cause already exists. | | **Prevention** | Known durable failure patterns are injected into the system prompt *before* the model picks a tool (`toolErrorProactiveInject`), scoped to the tools the session can actually call. Transient causes such as rate limits are never warned about in advance. The first occurrence of a failure is unavoidable; every later session is warned up front. | **Safety.** Every `add_quirk` and every content-changing `update_quirk` passes an immutable trust monitor that rejects destructive patterns (`rm -rf`, `force push`, `bypass security`). **Manual control from the CLI** ```bash opencode-rag quirk add "npm needs --legacy-peer-deps" --type gotcha --tag installation opencode-rag quirk list opencode-rag quirk update --content "..." --type decision opencode-rag quirk rm opencode-rag quirk lint # flag low-confidence, stale, or duplicate quirks opencode-rag quirk test "npm needs --legacy-peer-deps" ``` Manual `recall_quirks` calls use the looser `recallMinScore` (0.72). Raise it to 0.85 to keep unrelated quirks out of unrelated tasks. See the [plugin docs](doc/plugin.md#9-quirk-memory-experiential-memory) and the [CLI reference](doc/cli.md#quirk). ### 3. Decision model A small local model answers fast **classification, routing, policy, and scoring questions**, so the agent does not spend its own tokens on them. OpenCodeRAG uses Together AI's [tev1](https://ollama.com/library/tev1) via Ollama's `/v1/systemone` endpoint. Unlike chat models, tev1 scores a short `state` against 1 to 64 named questions and returns the chosen option with probabilities, typically in **40 to 150 ms warm**. | Question type | Use it for | Example | |---|---|---| | `choice` | Pick one of 2 to 24 options | "Which support intent is this?" → duplicate_charge / cancel / none | | `noul` | True/false probability | "Does the customer explicitly ask for a refund?" | | `score` | Place the input on a rubric | "How severe is this incident?" → cosmetic … critical | One call, two questions: ```json { "state": "Customer: I was charged twice for the October subscription ($19.99 each). Please refund the extra charge.", "questions": [ { "id": "intent", "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which support intent matches?", "criteria": { "duplicate_charge": "Charged more than once", "cancel": "Wants to cancel", "none": "None of the above" } }, { "id": "refund", "type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the customer explicitly ask for a refund?" } ] } ``` ``` Decision — ollama/tev1:0.8b - intent = duplicate_charge (confidence 0.97) - refund = true (p=0.96) ``` **Setup** ```bash ollama pull tev1:0.8b # 812 MB, fast: good for quick labels and CI ollama pull tev1:4b # 4.4 GB, more accurate: recommended for scoring ``` Requires Ollama ≥ 0.35. **Disabled by default.** Opt in via `decision.enabled`: ```json { "decision": { "enabled": true, "provider": "ollama", "model": "tev1:0.8b", "keepAlive": "30m", "routeBeforeAsking": false } } ``` `decision.baseUrl` accepts a root URL, an `/api`-suffixed URL, or an `/v1`-suffixed URL - both suffixes are stripped, so requests always go to `/v1/systemone`. Any server exposing that route works, for example **llama-swap**: ```json { "decision": { "enabled": true, "provider": "ollama", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:11437", "model": "Clef-Flash", "apiKey": "sk-llama-local" } } ``` `decision.apiKey` is sent as `Authorization: Bearer ` and is required when the server protects its routes (llama-swap's `api_key`). **Using it well** - Always include a `none` / "cannot be determined" option. - Keep `state` to the relevant excerpt (effective context is about 2k tokens). - Treat `confidence < ~0.3` as undecided. - Do not use it for factual recall, or as the only check for high-stakes decisions. **Pre-ask routing (optional).** With `decision.routeBeforeAsking: true`, the agent is told to resolve option choices through `make_decision` before asking you. It proceeds on a confident answer and asks only when the model is undecided or the choice is a matter of preference. Off by default. `opencode-rag decide` exposes the same engine from the CLI, and workspace setup creates a dedicated `make-decision` agent skill. See the [plugin docs](doc/plugin.md#make_decision) and the [configuration reference](doc/configuration.md#decision). ### 4. Shell Guard The same decision model can vet **every shell command before it runs**. With `shellGuard.enabled: true`, each `shell` / `bash` call is classified for destructive and malicious intent. If `p(destructive)` or `p(malicious)` reaches the threshold, the command is escalated to OpenCode's confirmation prompt together with the full verdict (probabilities plus a risk category). Otherwise it runs unchanged. ```json { "shellGuard": { "enabled": true, "threshold": 0.5, "timeoutMs": 10000, "onError": "allow" } } ``` | Aspect | Behavior | |---|---| | **Default** | Off. Enabling it adds one local model call to every shell command. | | **Speed** | A warm verdict takes about 200 to 230 ms. Example: `rm -rf ./dist` → 0.96 destructive; `ls -la src` → 0.23, allowed. | | **On failure** | Fail-open by default (`onError: "allow"`): if the classifier is down or times out, the command runs and a warning is logged. Set `"ask"` to require confirmation instead. | | **Cache** | Verdicts are cached for 10 minutes (256 entries). The key includes the provider and model, and cached probabilities are re-scored against the current threshold on every call. | | **Scope** | Put the block in `~/.config/opencode/opencode-rag.json` to apply it to every workspace. A workspace config can still override or disable it. | | **Live config** | Edits to `opencode-rag.json` apply without a restart. | | **Backend** | Defaults to the `decision` section. Any `/v1/systemone` endpoint works, for example llama-swap with `"baseUrl": "http://localhost:11437", "model": "Clef-Flash"`. | Every verdict is logged under `scope: shell.guard`, so you can tune the threshold against real commands. Shell Guard is a safety net, not a sandbox. See the [configuration reference](doc/configuration.md#shellguard) and the [plugin docs](doc/plugin.md#shell-guard-command-vetting). ### 5. Documentation and wiki modes Two optional modes turn the agent into a documentation maintainer. #### Documentation mode (`/doc`) Off by default. When `documentationMode.enabled` is `true`, the plugin adds a `/doc` slash command that drives the agent to add JSDoc/TSDoc comments to undocumented source files. No agent tools are registered; it works entirely through the slash command and a documentation system prompt. ```json { "documentationMode": { "enabled": true, "batchSize": 5 } } ``` **Workflow** 1. Type `/doc` to list all undocumented files, grouped by subdirectory. 2. The agent picks a subdirectory and documents every public symbol, preserving existing comments and implementation code. 3. Type `/doc src/auth/` to mark that subdirectory complete. Progress is saved in `.opencode/rag_db/doc-mode-progress.json`, so later sessions resume where you left off. See the [plugin docs](doc/plugin.md#5-documentation-mode--slash-command-doc). #### Wiki mode (`/wiki`) On by default. When `wikiMode.enabled` is `true`, the plugin injects a wiki-maintainer system prompt. The agent builds and maintains a persistent knowledge wiki in `.opencode/wiki/`: interlinked markdown pages that synthesize knowledge from the codebase, docs, and conversations. Two read-only agent tools make the mechanical wiki questions one-call answers instead of grep sweeps (registered when `wikiMode.tools` is `true`, the default): | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `wiki_graph` | Link-graph queries: backlinks, outlinks, neighborhood, orphans, dangling links, overview — rebuilt from the files on every call, so it is never stale | | `wiki_lint` | Deterministic health report: git-verified staleness (`sourceRefs` committed after `lastReviewed`), dead refs, uncommitted drift, structure, frontmatter and `index.md` coverage | The same engine backs a provider-free CLI (`opencode-rag wiki status/graph/lint`) and the `/wiki` slash command: | Command | Action | |---|---| | `/wiki` | Show wiki status (recursive page count, directories, index and log presence, graph health, latest log entry) | | `/wiki seed` | Generate the initial wiki from the README, file structure, and code patterns | | `/wiki lint` | Inject the computed deterministic report, then the agent handles judgment checks (contradictions, concepts lacking a page) and fixes findings | The agent maintains the pages during normal coding sessions; you do not write them yourself. The wiki lives in `.opencode/`, so it is git-trackable and every edit is a diff. See the [plugin docs](doc/plugin.md#6-wiki-mode--slash-command-wiki). ### 6. Image indexing Image files (PNG, JPEG, WebP, and others) are sent to a vision-capable LLM, and the generated descriptions are stored as searchable chunks. Visual assets then become discoverable with natural-language queries such as "login screen screenshot" or "architecture diagram". The `describe_image` tool also lets an agent inspect an image on demand. - **Providers:** Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and OpenCode Zen (`opencode` / `opencode-go`) compatible providers. - **On by default.** Set `imageDescription.enabled: false` to skip image files entirely. This is recommended if you have no vision model or no GPU. ### 7. Web UI, evaluation, and calibration **Web UI.** A browser dashboard for exploring the vector database: browse, visualize, and inspect chunks side-by-side with a movable splitter, edit the global and project configuration layers, switch between dark, plasma, drama, and light themes, and evaluate OpenCode sessions by retrieved chunks and consumed tokens. Launch it with `opencode-rag ui` (or let `opencode-rag setup` open it on the Configuration page). See the [Web UI docs](doc/webui.md). [![OpenCodeRAG Web UI](doc/assets/webui-3d.png)](doc/assets/webui-3d.png) **Does it actually save tokens?** Session-level analysis compares RAG-on against RAG-off, using tiktoken BPE (`cl100k_base`) for code tokenization: ```bash opencode-rag eval:sessions # list sessions opencode-rag eval:analyze # detailed breakdown opencode-rag eval:compare # side-by-side comparison ``` **Is retrieval good enough?** A separate harness measures quality: | Command | Purpose | |---|---| | `opencode-rag eval:gate` | Runs the labelled golden set and fails when Hit@5, MRR, or nDCG@10 drop below the documented floors | | `opencode-rag eval:decide` | Measures the decision model's accuracy, ECE, and Brier score on a labelled calibration set | | `opencode-rag eval:tune` | Sweeps the retrieval fusion weights against the golden set and reports the best configuration for your setup | The shipped `keywordWeight=0.4` is a default, not an optimum (on a code embedder it costs about 8 Hit@5 points), so measure instead of guessing. See the [evaluation docs](doc/evaluation.md). --- ## Tool reference ### MCP tools (plugin and MCP server) Inside OpenCode the plugin registers these in-process. Over MCP they are served by `opencode-rag mcp`. | Tool | What it does | When the agent uses it | |---|---|---| | `search_semantic` | Hybrid vector and keyword search over the indexed code | Before a code task, instead of reading whole files | | `get_file_skeleton` | AST outline of a file (functions, classes, methods) | To orient in a large file before reading it | | `find_usages` | Every reference to a symbol | Before editing a function, class, or variable | | `describe_image` | Describes an image with the configured vision model | When the task involves a screenshot, diagram, or other asset | | `make_decision` | Classifies, routes, or scores short text (needs `decision.enabled`) | When the answer reduces to a choice, a yes/no check, or a rubric score | ### Plugin-only tools (OpenCode) Registered by the OpenCode plugin, not served over MCP. | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | `recall_quirks` | Recalls stored gotchas, preferences, and decisions from past sessions | | `add_quirk` | Stores a new non-obvious fact, workaround, or convention | | `update_quirk` | Corrects a stored quirk that is outdated or wrong | | `delete_quirk` | Removes a quirk that is fixed, obsolete, or no longer applies | ### Slash commands and hotkeys (OpenCode) Default hotkeys and slash commands: | Input | Action | |---|---| | `Ctrl+Enter` | Append a relevant file list to the prompt | | `Ctrl+Alt+Enter` | Append full code chunks to the prompt | | `/rag-settings` or `Alt+S` | Open the settings panel | | `/doc` | Documentation mode (if enabled) | | `/wiki`, `/wiki seed`, `/wiki lint` | Wiki mode | Hotkeys can be changed via /rag-settings. --- ## Configuration Settings are stored as JSON (no comments). | File | Purpose | |---|---| | `.opencode/opencode-rag.json` | Workspace config (canonical) | | `~/.config/opencode/opencode-rag.json` | Machine-wide settings (Shell Guard, provider choices) inherited by every workspace | Shipped defaults: ```json { "embedding": { "provider": "ollama", "model": "qwen3-embedding:0.6b" }, "retrieval": { "topK": 20, "minScore": 0.35, "hybridSearch": { "enabled": true, "keywordWeight": 0.4, "symbolKeywordWeight": 0.6 } }, "shellGuard": { "enabled": false, "threshold": 0.5, "onError": "allow" }, "decision": { "enabled": false, "model": "tev1:4b" } } ``` The [configuration reference](doc/configuration.md) documents every option (embedding, indexing, retrieval, description, image description, decision, Shell Guard, plugin) and how the global and workspace layers merge. --- ## Privacy and security - **100% local by default.** Embeddings are generated locally via Ollama, and the vector database stays in your project directory. No source code or embeddings leave your machine unless you explicitly configure a third-party API. - **Shell Guard** sends command text only to the decision-model endpoint you configure (local Ollama or a local proxy). - **Decision model** is only asked about short excerpts that you or the agent pass in. - **Quirk memory** writes pass an immutable trust monitor that rejects destructive patterns. --- ## Limitations - **Retrieval quality depends on the embedding model.** Small CPU-friendly models trade accuracy for speed. Measure with `eval:gate` and `eval:tune` rather than assuming a default. - **Image descriptions need a vision model.** This is a feature that meaningfully wants a GPU to be pleasant. Disable it with `imageDescription.enabled: false` if you have none. - **Shell Guard costs one model call per shell command** (about 200 ms warm) and fails open by default. It is a safety net, not a sandbox. - **The decision model supports only Ollama's `/v1/systemone` endpoint** for now. - **ClickHouse is opt-in** and needs a running server. LanceDB is the default and needs no separate installation. --- ## Documentation index This README is the entry point.
